title: PBS Compared Trump’s January “All Promises Kept” Claim With PolitiFact Ratings
description_medium: PolitiFact reported that Trump told a January Detroit audience, “I’ve kept all my promises,” while its MAGA-Meter tracked 75 second-term campaign pledges. In a February 23 assessment, about 19% were marked kept and 45% in progress; others were stalled, broken or compromises. The source supports that comparison, but not the record’s March 4 date or a statement made that day.
description_long: President Donald Trump told a Detroit audience in January 2026, “I’ve kept all my promises, and much more.” PBS NewsHour reported on February 23 that PolitiFact’s MAGA-Meter followed 75 of Trump’s second-term campaign pledges. At that time, PolitiFact rated about 19% as kept and about 45% as in progress, while the remainder included stalled, broken, or compromise ratings. The scorecard therefore showed a range of outcomes among the promises it tracked, rather than universal completion. The tracker’s categories are dated assessments, not a final judgment on every commitment Trump made. The PBS article describes the statement as occurring in January and the report itself as February 23; this record is dated March 4. The source does not document a new March 4 statement or messaging event. The comparison is supported, but the event date and claim of certainty require clarification against the source chronology.
evidence_notes: PBS/PolitiFact support January Detroit quote and February 23 tracker snapshot. Record date is March 4; no later statement in the source.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: PBS Compared Trump’s January “All Promises Kept” Claim With PolitiFact Ratings
exact_blocker: The source documents a January statement and February 23 report, not a March 4 statement; the record date does not align.

title: NPR Reported Federal Agencies Removed Climate and Environmental Terms From Public Materials
description_medium: NPR reported in April 2025 that climate- and environment-related terms, including “climate crisis” and “environmental justice,” were disappearing from some federal websites and documents. Researchers at federally funded institutions said they were advised to avoid phrases such as “climate change” and “biodiversity” in grant language. The White House denied creating a banned-word list, saying agencies interpreted executive orders.
description_long: In April 2025, NPR reported that words and phrases including “climate crisis,” “climate science,” “clean energy,” and “environmental justice” were being removed from some federal websites and documents. The reporting also described researchers at federally funded institutions who said they had been advised to avoid terms such as “climate change,” “sustainable,” and “biodiversity” in grant applications. Some researchers said they changed their wording because they feared jeopardizing funding. The White House denied that it had created a list of prohibited terms and said federal agencies were interpreting the president’s executive orders. NPR reported that the White House, NIH, and HHS did not answer its specific questions about why particular words were targeted. The article documents reported language changes and researchers’ concerns, alongside the administration’s denial of a central list. It does not show a universal rule banning hundreds of terms across every federal document, nor does it establish that all researchers or agencies followed the same practice. The event is a reported shift in agency communications and research language, not an enacted nationwide statutory ban.
evidence_notes: NPR describes specific terminology removals and researcher concerns; White House denied creating a list and said agencies interpret EOs. Separates PEN analysis/proposal from agency implementation.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: NPR Reported Federal Agencies Removed Climate and Environmental Terms From Public Materials

title: NPR Found More Than 50 Epstein File Pages Missing From DOJ’s Public Database
description_medium: NPR reported that more than 50 pages of FBI interview records and notes associated with an unverified allegation involving Donald Trump were not in DOJ’s public Epstein-files database. NPR compared serial numbers in the database with FBI case files and discovery logs. Trump denies wrongdoing; the report does not verify the allegation or establish that he controlled the department’s release decisions.
description_long: NPR’s February 24, 2026, investigation found that the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database appeared to be missing more than 50 pages of FBI interview records and notes associated with an unverified allegation involving Donald Trump. NPR compared serial numbers appearing before and after the pages in the public database with FBI case records, emails, and discovery logs from a batch of documents published at the end of January. The records included interviews concerning a woman who said she had been sexually abused as a minor and later made an allegation about Trump. That allegation remains unverified; Trump denies wrongdoing, and the reporting does not establish that it is true. The department cited privilege and duplication among reasons material may be withheld. NPR also described files connected to a separate witness in Ghislaine Maxwell’s case that had been removed and later restored. The investigation documented a gap between public access and records indicated by serial-number sequences and logs. It did not show that President Trump directed the handling of files or that NPR’s findings changed his public messaging.
evidence_notes: NPR details >50 pages, serial-number/log comparison, allegation attribution and separate records restored. Removes unsupported narrative effect.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: NPR Found More Than 50 Epstein File Pages Missing From DOJ’s Public Database

title: AP Timeline: Trump Criticized Iran Nuclear Talks Three Hours Before Strike Order
description_medium: AP’s March 2, 2026, timeline says Trump told reporters Friday afternoon that he was dissatisfied with Iran nuclear talks. Three hours later, he ordered the operation that began with U.S.-Israeli strikes early February 28. The timeline reports a short interval between public comments and the order, but does not establish whether deliberations or oversight were accelerated or bypassed.
description_long: The Associated Press’s March 2 account traced the hours before the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. On the afternoon of Friday, February 27, President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he was not pleased with the way nuclear negotiations were progressing. AP reported that three hours later Trump gave the order for the military operation, which began early the next morning. The strikes killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior officials. The reported sequence connects public doubt about the talks with the decision to use force in a matter of hours, while leaving the internal planning process largely separate from the published timeline. It does not show which options officials considered in those three hours, who advised Trump, or what congressional oversight had occurred. The event supports a close chronology, not the conclusion that executive momentum outpaced deliberation. The decisive fact in AP’s account is the three-hour interval between Trump’s public comment and his order, followed by a major escalation in the conflict.
evidence_notes: Same AP timeline as 1447/1472; distinct record proposition concerns deliberative oversight and should not assert it was bypassed.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: AP Timeline: Trump Criticized Iran Nuclear Talks Three Hours Before Strike Order

title: Trump Ordered Iran Strikes Hours After Publicly Criticizing Nuclear Talks
description_medium: On February 27, 2026, Trump told reporters that he was unhappy with Iran nuclear negotiations. AP’s timeline says he ordered military action three hours later; U.S.-Israeli strikes began early February 28 and killed Iran’s supreme leader and other senior officials. The account documents timing and outcome, but does not describe advisers’ private views or show that loyalty displaced dissent.
description_long: An Associated Press timeline places President Donald Trump’s order to strike Iran three hours after he told reporters at the White House that he was unhappy with the nuclear talks. The comments came on the afternoon of February 27, 2026; the joint U.S.-Israeli operation began early on February 28. AP reported that the strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian officials. This chronology shows how quickly the administration moved from public criticism of negotiations to military action. It does not reveal what advisers recommended during those hours, whether there was internal disagreement, or whether Trump preferred loyal alignment over open challenge. Nor does it establish that the timing was selected for political advantage. The account documents the public comment, order, and immediate outcome, while the internal deliberation process remains outside the facts provided in the timeline. A factual title can capture the short interval without suggesting that the president suppressed advice or dissent.
evidence_notes: Uses AP’s three-hour chronology and strike outcome; no evidence about private advisers or internal dissent.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: Trump Ordered Iran Strikes Hours After Publicly Criticizing Nuclear Talks

title: Guardian Reported DOJ Omitted Three FBI Memos From First Epstein Files Release
description_medium: The Guardian said three FBI interview memoranda from 2019, documenting four interviews, were absent from DOJ’s first public Epstein-files release and later obtained by the newspaper. One included an unsubstantiated allegation involving Trump; he denies wrongdoing. DOJ said the omitted records were duplicative or privileged, and lawmakers sought answers. The reporting documents a release dispute, not a specific Trump “conflict narrative.”
description_long: The Guardian reported on February 26, 2026, that it obtained three FBI Form 302 memoranda documenting four interviews conducted in 2019 about allegations involving Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. The Justice Department had not included those three records in its initial public release, although another earlier interview was available. An administration official confirmed the memos were authentic. The allegations they describe remain unsubstantiated, and Trump denies wrongdoing; the existence of investigative notes is not proof that the alleged conduct occurred. DOJ said the unpublished material was duplicative or privileged, while Democratic lawmakers on the House Oversight Committee sought an explanation for its absence. The report also discussed a separate civil lawsuit against Epstein’s estate that the accuser later dropped; that proceeding does not determine the truth of the claims in the FBI memoranda. The documented event is a dispute about which records the public release included and why three authenticated memos were omitted. The story does not identify a specific ongoing Trump narrative or prove that he directed the disclosure decisions.
evidence_notes: Guardian article supports missing memos, authenticity, DOJ rationale and oversight response. Allegations are unsubstantiated and attributed.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: Guardian Reported DOJ Omitted Three FBI Memos From First Epstein Files Release

title: At Least 16 Epstein Files Disappeared From DOJ’s Public Webpage in December 2025
description_medium: AP reported that at least 16 Epstein-related files posted to the Justice Department’s public webpage were no longer available the next day. The missing files included a photograph showing Donald Trump with Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump and Ghislaine Maxwell. DOJ said it would continue reviewing and redacting materials but did not explain the specific removals. The report documents missing web access, not a chain-of-custody breach.
description_long: The Justice Department published a batch of Epstein-related files on December 19, 2025. Less than a day later, at least 16 files were no longer accessible on its public webpage, the Associated Press reported. Among the missing items was a photograph showing Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, Melania Trump, and Ghislaine Maxwell; other missing material included images of paintings. DOJ did not answer AP’s questions about why the files disappeared or whether the removals were intentional. The department later said on X that photographs and other material would continue to be reviewed and redacted as it received new information. That statement did not account for the specific missing files. The public-facing change raised questions about transparency in a release that had already drawn scrutiny, but the reporting does not identify who made the changes or prove that the underlying government records were destroyed, altered, or removed from custody. The title’s phrase “chain-of-custody suspicion” is an inference beyond the article’s findings. AP documents a gap in the webpage and an incomplete explanation, not a forensic failure.
evidence_notes: AP/PBS details: at least 16 gone next day, includes Trump photo, DOJ generic statement but no specific explanation. No underlying-record custody evidence.

title: Trump Established White House Faith Office With Role in Foster Care and Adoption Partnerships
description_medium: On February 7, 2025, Executive Order 14205 established the White House Faith Office and directed it to promote partnerships between faith-based organizations and government programs, including foster care and adoption. The order also said federal agencies should protect religious liberty and end religious discrimination. It did not itself authorize federally funded providers to reject LGBTQ+ applicants or revoke nondiscrimination guidance.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14205 on February 7, 2025, establishing the White House Faith Office within the Executive Office of the President. The order tasked the office with coordinating engagement between federal agencies and faith-based entities, community organizations, and houses of worship. Its stated areas of focus included strengthening families, protecting religious liberty, and promoting foster-care and adoption programs in partnership with faith-based organizations. The order also directed the executive branch to enforce constitutional religious-liberty protections and end religious discrimination by the federal government. It did not itself authorize federally funded foster-care agencies to refuse LGBTQ+ applicants, nor did the supplied sources identify an operative repeal of nondiscrimination guidance. The order’s emphasis on faith-based partnerships became part of broader debates about religious liberty and LGBTQ+ equality, but the policy’s effect depends on implementing rules and program-specific safeguards. The event documented here is the establishment and remit of the White House office, not an express federal authorization of discriminatory placement practices. The original description overstated what the order directly did and misidentified its legal operation.
evidence_notes: EO 14205 official text establishes office and foster-care/adoption partnership role; does not itself authorize provider exclusion. Corrects conflated claims.
corrected_wording: Proposed title wording: Trump Established White House Faith Office With Role in Foster Care and Adoption Partnerships
